papers.title: GazeRIB: Systematic Evaluation of Multi-Reader Gaze-Guided Chest X-ray Learning
papers.authors: Nattakorn Kittisut, Roy M. Gabriel, Marly van Assen, Mohammadreza Zandehshahvar et al.
papers.summary: Radiologists' visual attention can supervise medical image learning, but how reader panel composition affects its value remains untested. We evaluated GazeRIB (Gaze-guided Radiologist-Informed Blackout), which masks unviewed regions during training and uses unmasked images at inference. Eight experts repeatedly read the same 80 chest X-rays (CXRs). We compared individual readers with three-, five- and eight-reader panels across seven architectures and 10 seeds, evaluating 910 models on a separate 2,897-CXR cohort for four-class severity prediction. Every panel improved macro F1 over the no-gaze baseline by 5.33-7.47 percentage points (pp; Bonferroni-adjusted p < 0.007); no individual reader reached significance on this endpoint. Three readers captured 73-80% of the eight-reader gain in macro F1, the area under the receiver-operating-characteristic curve (ROC-AUC) and the area under the precision-recall curve (AU-PRC). On external validation without retraining, all four panels improved ROC-AUC on SIIM-FISABIO-RSNA by +1.93 to +4.24 pp (p <= 0.004); on MIMIC-Eye no panel differed significantly from baseline, whereas the single-reader average declined (-1.40 pp, p = 0.008). Reader composition therefore influenced performance, although transfer depended on the cohort.

papers.title: Latent Reasoning in Continuous Space for Unified Multimodal Models
papers.authors: Byungwoo Jeon, Yoonwoo Jeong, Hyunseok Lee, Minsu Cho et al.
papers.summary: Unified Multimodal Models (UMMs) achieve remarkable success on diverse multimodal understanding and generation tasks, yet they still struggle to effectively leverage language-based chain-of-thought reasoning for image generation. As a result, existing reasoning-augmented UMMs often fail to inherit the test-time scaling and fine-grained controllability observed in large language models. We attribute this failure to a fundamental modality mismatch: reasoning is performed in a discrete token space, whereas image generation operates in a continuous space. To bridge this gap, we introduce a Latent Reasoning framework in Continuous space (LARC), which alleviates the token-level bottleneck by reasoning over continuous hidden states. Specifically, the training framework consists of two stages: (i) curriculum supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and (ii) information-gain reinforcement learning (RL). First, the curriculum SFT stage gradually converts token-level reasoning into latent reasoning. Subsequently, the information-gain RL stage self-evolves latent reasoning without ground truth supervision. Experiments across diverse text-to-image generation benchmarks show that LARC consistently improves generation quality, prompt following, and compositional fidelity. Notably, LARC achieves state-of-the-art performance on GenEval with a 7%p gain over BAGEL and demonstrates clear test-time scaling behavior, outperforming token-based generation under both parallel and sequential test-time scaling strategies.

papers.title: Flide: Accelerating Decision Inference with Exact State Forking
papers.authors: Bobo Li, Jiajia Song, Hao Fei, Wynne Hsu et al.
papers.summary: Decision models such as Jev have emerged as a highly promising paradigm for LLM agent systems, providing lightweight and reliable categorical reasoning for rapid System One execution. However, existing generation-oriented inference engines fail to support these workloads effectively, suffering from severe prefix recomputation overheads or distorted output probabilities. To address this challenge, we propose Flide, an efficient and exact inference engine that decouples the logical tree structure of a decision request from its physical execution within a single flattened token stream. Through ForkAttention, Flide navigates request dependencies using GPU-resident indices across both standard attention and recurrent Gated DeltaNet layers, guaranteeing in exact arithmetic that every query branch evaluates identically to an isolated forward pass. By expressing branch topologies directly in GPU-resident metadata, Flide accommodates diverse request mixtures with a compact set of pre-recorded execution graphs while enabling expanding agent histories to resume from checkpoints saved in earlier passes. Extensive evaluations on public hybrid and decision models demonstrate that Flide answers queries up to 9.5 times faster than vLLM and SGLang while staying closest to a float32 reference in total variation distance. By unifying physical execution throughput with mathematical exactness, Flide establishes a principled foundation for scalable, latency-critical decision intelligence in agent systems.

papers.title: Latent Sparse Attention: Towards Subquadratic Ultra-Long Context Attention
papers.authors: Ales Kubicek, Andrea Caciolai, Liangzu Peng, Sukrit Sumant et al.
papers.summary: Agentic workflows are increasingly shifting towards long-horizon tasks, such as open-ended scientific work, where models benefit from long context windows. However, at ultra-long context (above 1M tokens), full attention is prohibitively expensive. A promising approach is sparse attention, in which a dedicated indexer selects a subset of keys for the attention. Yet current methods of indexing either still have quadratic cost in context size or lose accuracy at ultra-long context scale. We address this with Latent Sparse Attention (LSA), an efficient attention method that maintains accuracy at ultra-long context. In LSA, keys are hierarchically clustered in a learned latent space, and queries score the hierarchy of clusters instead of scoring every key, making prefill, decode and training faster at long context. We propose two variants, Distilled-LSA (D-LSA), which can be applied to pre-trained models via distillation, and Native-LSA (N-LSA), which is trained natively on the next-token loss alone. On GLM-5.3-FLASH (QWEN-3.8-27B) at 10M tokens, D-LSA speeds up one attention layer by 22.7x (72.4x) in prefill and 4.6x (42.5x) in decode over its original sparse attention (full attention), while keeping similar accuracy across a variety of tasks. N-LSA matches the accuracy of full attention with a training speedup of 1.6x per layer at 128k tokens. LSA offers practical and efficient attention for models to benefit from ultra-long context.

papers.title: Hierarchical World Models with Implicit Dynamics
papers.authors: Gaoyue Zhou, Yvonne Wu, Zichen Jeff Cui, Nicolas Ballas et al.
papers.summary: Planning with world models enables test-time adaptation for embodied agents, offering superior generalization over direct policy learning. However, long-horizon tasks remain hindered by cumulative errors and search complexity. Existing hierarchical methods often use rigid macro-actions or latent skills, leading to brittle representations and limited fine-grained control. We introduce ID-WM (Implicit Dynamics World Models), a hierarchical world model that decouples state-space reachability from local control. Our framework utilizes a high-level model to sample feasible transitions across the state manifold and a low-level world model as an inverse dynamics solver to ground these transitions into precise actions. This allows the planner to identify reachable subgoals without being constrained by low-level execution details. By prioritizing local physical feasibility over global behavioral patterns, ID-WM synthesizes novel long-horizon plans from short segments, transcending the specific behavioral modes seen during training. We demonstrate its effectiveness across three navigation and manipulation suites, achieving a 38.5% improvement over state-of-the-art policy and diffusion-based planners. Crucially, by leveraging this hierarchical structure to mitigate compounding errors, our approach yields a 135% performance gain over single-level world model MPC, particularly in complex, unseen configurations for long-horizon tasks. Videos can be viewed at https://id-wm.github.io

papers.title: SemEllipsoid: Semantic-aware Shape Abstraction with Ellipsoid
papers.authors: Kuankuan Cheng, Haocheng Yuan, Changjian Li
papers.summary: Representing 3D shapes using a set of primitives - known as shape abstraction - is an actively studied problem in computer graphics with wide applications in shape understanding, analysis, and simulation due to the compactness and computational efficiency of the primitive-based representation. Prior work has primarily focused on geometry-aware shape abstraction, where the objective is to approximate the input shape with a minimal set of primitives while preserving geometric fidelity. However, these methods often overlook semantic consistency, inevitably leading to primitives that span across multiple semantic parts. Such inconsistency can cause undesirable artifacts in downstream tasks such as part-level shape editing or manipulation. In this paper, we introduce a new task - semantic-aware shape abstraction, where the goal is to produce abstractions that are both geometrically faithful and semantically consistent, ensuring that each primitive adheres strictly to a single semantic part without crossing semantic boundaries. We propose SemEllipsoid, a novel method to address this problem using ellipsoidal primitives. The core idea is to inject semantic constraints into the primitive optimization process leveraging the availability of semantic cues from large-scale foundation models. We design a fully differentiable projection-blending-evaluation scheme to measure semantic divergence against input semantic masks, and formulate an alternating optimization strategy to iteratively solve for optimal semantic assignment and primitive configurations. Our method is non-learning-based, requiring no data collection or network training, and generalizes well to shapes from arbitrary categories. It also supports different levels of abstraction according to user demand. Extensive experiments and evaluations validate the effectiveness of our approach across several 3D shape collections.

papers.title: Dittany: Contribution-Guided Repair Framework for MAS Applications
papers.authors: Hanqi Sun, Yuchen Shao, Hanyi Si, Beibei Xu et al.
papers.summary: LLM-based multi-agent system (MAS) applications can produce useful intermediate results while leaving task requirements unsatisfied. Repairing such executions requires identifying the work still needed and the completed results that can support it. We present , a contribution-guided runtime repair framework for MAS applications. derives expected contributions and acceptance conditions from task requirements and method specifications, and connects their dependencies in a contribution graph. Runtime checks locate unmet conditions and establish which results remain usable. These results guide action-level correction when available inputs suffice, or graph-level recovery when prerequisites or unfinished work need revision. Both repair scopes retain validated contributions and check repaired outputs before subsequent work uses them. We evaluate on 30 applications across six MAS frameworks and 9,000 tasks. It detects runtime failures with 88.28% precision and 79.18% recall, and achieves 84.76% task accuracy, improving over Native execution by 26.74 percentage points and the strongest of four recovery baselines by 21.28 points. Estimated deployment token consumption is 17.92% above Native, but 24.19% below Reflexion and 13.05% below Iterative Rollback. Ablation results show that combining the two repair scopes achieves higher accuracy and lower token consumption than graph-level repair alone.

papers.title: RoboArchitect: Automating the Design of Robotic Agents with Persistent Memory
papers.authors: Shengguang Wu, Suning Huang, Cherie Ho, Ria Doshi et al.
papers.summary: Recent work shows that a frozen robot policy performs far better inside an agent harness, where control code decides when to query the policy, consult vision tools, or command the arm directly. Yet today these harnesses are built by hand and redesigned for each new robot or benchmark. We show that harness design can be automated, offering a strong alternative to finetuning on a novel setup. In RoboArchitect, a coding model observes a robot's rollouts, diagnoses failures, and iteratively revises the harness around the frozen policy. The harness evolves on a set of episodes for its optimization and is evaluated on held-out scenes and tasks. Without updating any model weights, RoboArchitect raises average success from 9.7% to 43.3% on unseen scenes (4.5x) and from 12.7% to 40.2% on unseen tasks (3.2x), across multiple benchmarks and policies. The gains are largest where the benchmark is far from the policy's training data: wrapping a general-purpose policy, the evolved harness yields a specialist that often outperforms even the finetuned version. Intuitive control strategies are automatically designed, such as lifting a jammed arm clear or reaching in horizontally when an obstacle blocks the way from above. The harness also evolves its own persistent memory, carrying learned experience, such as effective grasp depths, into later decisions. These results suggest that substantial headroom in robotic manipulation lies in the agent harness, and its design can be effectively automated and optimized without weight updates.

papers.title: Counting on Dummies: Privacy Amplification with Observable Counts and Truncated Batches
papers.authors: Vitaly Feldman, Audra McMillan, Kunal Talwar
papers.summary: In many practical deployments of Differentially Private Stochastic Gradient Descent (DP-SGD), the server processes data in batches. Randomly sampling these batches allows for better privacy bounds via privacy amplification results. Most sampling schemes with provable privacy amplification, including Poisson sampling and random allocation, result in variable batch sizes. The privacy guarantee of these schemes requires that the batch sizes are not revealed. In distributed settings, the server performing the aggregation or any party observing the communication traffic may learn these batch sizes. Furthermore, in both centralized and distributed settings, memory and computation constraints may require each batch to be of some maximum size s, necessitating truncation of the batch when it exceeds this limit. It is known that this truncation can result in a significant increase in privacy loss. In this work, we address both of these challenges via a simple mechanism that uses a random number of dummy points to privatize the batch size and maintain the privacy guarantee even under truncation. We demonstrate that our mechanism is easy to implement in a distributed setting, and provide a general analysis of this mechanism for both Poisson sampling and random allocation. Our analysis is designed to support efficient and relatively tight privacy accounting. It also effectively amplifies the privacy of the count releases by subsampling, making the expected number of dummy points asymptotically smaller than what is needed to directly privatize the (sensitivity-one) batch sizes with non-negative noise. For Poisson sampling with truncated batches, we demonstrate empirically that our mechanism achieves better privacy–efficiency tradeoffs than the direct accounting for truncation recently given by (Ganesh, 2025).

papers.title: ReLift: Dense 3D Tracking as Lifted Trajectory Repair
papers.authors: Assaf Singer, Maroun Khriesh, Noam Rotstein, Yoni Kasten et al.
papers.summary: Dense 3D tracking from monocular video requires establishing point correspondences over time, estimating their depth, and inferring their trajectories during occlusion. Existing methods typically learn these tasks jointly, a demanding objective given the scarcity of 4D supervision. We show that strong pretrained 2D trackers and 3D geometry models provide an effective foundation: lifted trajectories, with occluded segments simply interpolated, already rival dedicated 3D trackers using the same geometry. However, lifted trajectories inherit correspondence and depth errors, and under occlusion, their depth comes from the occluder rather than the tracked point. We introduce ReLift, an efficient feed-forward framework that recasts dense 3D tracking as geometric trajectory repair and completion. At its core, a trajectory corrector alternates attention along and across trajectories to preserve reliable observations, repair corrupted positions, and complete missing motion. Using only geometric inputs allows us to train directly on 3D trajectories with simulated lifting errors, decoupling training from images and from any specific tracker or geometry model. Concentrating 4D supervision on trajectory refinement yields a reusable model that consistently improves lifted trajectories across trackers and geometry providers without retraining, so it benefits directly from future advances in either component. On WorldTrack, ReLift achieves state-of-the-art mean accuracy, improving on the strongest baselines by 2.1 APD on all points and 3.0 on dynamic points, with faster configurations remaining competitive with leading 3D trackers while running faster than 4RC. Visit our supplementry page for more examples and code.

papers.title: ROOF: Learning Humanoid Fall Recovery under Overhead Constraints
papers.authors: Yidan Lu, Jiayuan Yu, Zongrui Cai, Jingwen Sun et al.
papers.summary: A fallen humanoid beneath an overhead obstacle faces a coupled recovery problem. It must create clearance while organizing support for a stable rise, since attempting to stand before making room can further increase obstruction. We introduce a reinforcement learning method with contact-supported geometric escape guidance, which rewards incremental reduction of robot-obstacle overlap without prescribing an escape path. To achieve this, a learned motion prior, together with posture-dependent support and joint-stall costs, is proposed to shape a single policy that learns when to clear the obstacle, how to establish support, and when to complete the rise, all using proprioception alone. In simulation, it recovers in 88.5% of trials beneath plates that can only be lifted, compared with 18.9% without geometric guidance, and in 98.6% of trials beneath free plates with randomized size, mass and placement. On a Unitree G1, the deployed policy recovered in 95 of 150 attempts across seven real-world obstacle scenes, including furniture and multi-object arrangements absent from training. Project page: https://lu-yidan.github.io/ROOF/

papers.title: A General Theoretical Framework for Transformed Geometric Pattern Matching in Music
papers.authors: David Meredith
papers.summary: In this paper, we present a framework of concepts, terminology and notation for geometric pattern matching, centred around the idea of a transformation class. After formally defining the concept of a transformation class, we provide detailed definitions of a number of specific transformation classes that are particularly relevant to pattern matching and pattern discovery in music, which is the primary application domain within which the framework has been developed. We then provide formal definitions of the notions of match, occurrence, maximal match\/ and maximal occurrence\/ and prove some results relating to these concepts. We then define and explore in detail the idea of an occurrence set\/ and the more general notion of a heterogeneous occurrence set. Finally, we explore in detail the concept of transformational equivalence, including a consideration of transformation groups, along with the group-theoretic and transformational equivalence properties of selected transformation classes.

papers.title: RAMA: Retrieval-Augmented Multi-Agent Routing with Episodic Memory for LEO Satellite Networks
papers.authors: Xin Ming Li, Peng Hu
papers.summary: Low-Earth orbit (LEO) satellite networks present a challenging routing environment due to rapidly changing topology, traffic, and link conditions. Existing deep reinforcement learning (DRL) routing methods typically rely on current observations and information encoded in network weights, limiting their ability to exploit successful past experiences. We propose RAMA, a retrieval-augmented multi-agent DRL framework with Approximate Information State (AIS), in which each satellite combines its local observation, recent routing history, neighboring state information, and retrieved entries from a per-satellite episodic memory. Retrieved experiences are integrated through a Transformer-based decision network trained with AIS-based auxiliary objectives. With weights frozen in a 140-satellite Kepler constellation, RAMA reduces mean end-to-end latency by 13.4% and 99th-percentile latency by 66.7% relative to the state-of-theart double deep Q-network (DDQN) routing method, mainly by avoiding long detours. Updated online, RAMA remains stable while DDQN degrades. On the 1,584-satellite Starlink shell 1, the reduction in mean latency grows to 93.2%, and updating RAMA online lowers its mean latency by a further 25.5%. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of retrieval-augmented memory for scalable decentralized routing in LEO satellite networks.

papers.title: REA: A Routed Embodied Agent Runtime for Asynchronous Brain-Cerebellum Control
papers.authors: Pengfei Zhou, Yixing Ma, Zhengfeiyang Zhang, Haoyuan Chen et al.
papers.summary: Foundation models are becoming remarkably reliable at high-level reasoning, yet they remain too slow and costly to serve as fine-grained controllers. Conversely, fast policies like VLAs and whole-body controllers offer more efficient reflexes, but struggle to generalize. While pairing a deliberative brain (foundation models) with a reactive cerebellum (fast policies) seems natural for embodied systems, two obstacles remain: methods are built and scored on incompatible stacks, and their asynchronous coordination is difficult. For example, an agent that calls the VLA in the agentic loop can stall the fast execution, while a VLA that calls the agent on errors tends to re-trigger fallbacks repeatedly or completely miss silent failures. To address this, we propose REA (Routed Embodied Agent), a unified runtime where a deliberative System 2, an embodied router System 1 and reactive System 0 policies cooperate under a single golden rule - no running policy waits on the brain. Instead of querying the brain at each failure, REA employs a route memory that stores each policy's measured success ahead of time, a boundary-triggered judge gate that consults the brain on policy execution, and a shared-budget escalation ladder for bounded recovery. Evaluated on 3,000 test episodes across 60 LIBERO-Pro tasks, REA reaches 95.9% success and beats the best single-agent baseline in its own policy pool (94.7%) while reducing control steps by 25% and control time by 17%. In a separate 100-episode RoboTwin 2.0 study, REA achieves 84% success with VLA policies and 86% with VLA+code, compared with 80% for the strongest single VLA baseline MEDex. These results demonstrate learned and programmatic policies operating within the same runtime. REA also transfers to BEHAVIOR-1K and a real Unitree G1 humanoid, achieving the highest observed success among the compared methods.

papers.title: A Hybrid Path Planning Framework for Assistive Wheelchair Navigation in Dynamic Pedestrian Environments
papers.authors: Damla Leblebicioğlu, Rachel Barume, Taşkın Padır
papers.summary: Autonomous wheelchairs can improve the quality of life for individuals with mobility impairments by providing greater independence. However, reliable navigation especially in human environments is a major challenge due to factors such as dynamic obstacles, unpredictable pedestrian behavior, and the users' need to complete multiple stops along the way before reaching their final destination. This paper presents a hybrid path planning framework for multi-goal navigation in dynamic environments. The framework integrates the Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP) for global task ordering with the Potential Field (PF) method and heuristic local planners such as Rapidly-exploring Random Tree (RRT) and A-star (A*) to achieve collision-free navigation. Within this hybrid framework, TSP determines the visiting order of intermediate stations, PF transfers global path information, and local planners avoid obstacles while guiding the robot to the stations. The local planners generate feasible paths that allow the robot to follow the global trajectory and reroute to avoid static and dynamic obstacles. For this purpose, two algorithms have been developed: (i) TSP-PF-RRT and (ii) TSP-PF-A*. The performance of the proposed algorithms are evaluated using Monte Carlo simulations in crowded and extra-crowded scenarios that contain heterogeneous dynamic and static obstacles. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed hybrid framework enables efficient multi-goal navigation while maintaining safe operation in dynamic environments with humans, with TSP-PF-RRT achieving fewer or no collisions and shorter travel distances.

papers.title: Proof-Carrying Evolution: Black-Box Search, White-Box Flight
papers.authors: Amit Jain, Sergio Sanchez-Hurtado, Victor Rodriguez-Fernandez, Richard Linares
papers.summary: We study whether a language model can help design controllers whose behavior can be formally checked. In proof-carrying evolution (PCE), a search proposes controllers together with their certificates. Their mathematical forms are fixed; a proposer chooses their numerical parameters together. Certificate checks guide selection, and only a certified candidate can be returned. The deployed artifact is a control law and its certificate; the language model is used only during design. We compare four language models with classical search and synthesis on docking under a speed limit, pursuit of a maneuvering target, and attitude control on SO(3), using paired runs and shared proposal allowances. Certificates are checked in exact rational arithmetic during search on the linear problems. On SO(3), the search uses floating-point checks, followed by exact re-verification of every reported champion. The best run of each method also receives Lean 4 proofs of its stated control properties. On the linear problems, the strongest models beat the standard classical baselines on every run, but a classical optimizer that chooses certificates for the same objective closes most of that lead. Among the cited pursuit champions, the ranking does not survive a change from Euler to zero-order-hold dynamics. On SO(3), no model detectably outperforms CMA-ES when mixed with classical mutation. When models write every proposal, one tested model improves on CMA-ES and the other performs worse than its mixed variant. All search medians remain below the hand-tuned law. In a docking control with the objective and mutation operator held fixed, retaining certified candidates yields new certified designs in every run; removing this rule yields none.

papers.title: Beyond Smart Homes: Characterizing IoT Vulnerabilities Across Sectors, Vendors, and Products
papers.authors: Tina Rezaei, Suzan Bayhan, Andrea Continella, Jeroen van der Ham-de Vos et al.
papers.summary: The Internet of Things (IoT) has expanded beyond consumer smart homes to sectors, such as industrial systems, healthcare, and smart cities, broadening the IoT attack surface. Prior empirical work has focused on studying aggregate IoT vulnerability characteristics or specific protocols, so patching is directed by aggregate security guidance. However, if dominant weaknesses differ substantially across sectors or products, such uniform guidance misdirects the remediation effort. To address this gap, we present a fine-grained, data-driven analysis of IoT vulnerabilities using a dataset of more than 15,000 IoT specific CVEs. We design a pipeline to enrich noisy CPE (Common Platform Enumeration) metadata, normalizing vendors and products, then assigning product type and sector labels using lexical matching, fuzzy clustering, and LLM-assisted classification. We find meaningful differences in the weakness profile of IoT sectors. For example, healthcare is dominated by authentication and credential weaknesses, while automotive faces memory issues. More importantly, we find that weakness profiles are more similar across different product types from the same vendor than across the same product type built by different vendors. This suggests vendor-level factors such as shared code and development practices dominate weakness inheritance, making a vendor's disclosure history informative about its other products. Our findings suggest weakness classes should be used to prioritize remediation efforts.

papers.title: AutoAnalysis: An automated, self-updating meta-analysis of human-AI collaboration
papers.authors: Michelle Vaccaro, Abdullah Almaatouq, Thomas W. Malone
papers.summary: As generative artificial intelligence (AI) becomes more capable and widely used, understanding when and how humans should work with these systems is becoming increasingly important. However, the empirical evidence in this space offers conflicting recommendations, which leaves individuals and organizations without clear guidance on when to combine human and AI capabilities. Existing meta-analyses can help reconcile these findings, but they require substantial manual effort and cannot readily incorporate new evidence as it emerges. To address this challenge, we introduce AutoAnalysis: an automated, self-updating meta-analysis of when humans and AI work better together, and when they work better alone. AutoAnalysis' most recent run synthesizes 1,955 effect sizes from 420 papers. Across this body of work, we found that, on average, human-AI combinations performed significantly better than humans alone, but they performed significantly worse than the better of humans or AI alone. These findings highlight the important distinction between improving human performance and achieving human-AI synergy and underscore the need to evaluate collaboration against both human and AI performance alone. As new studies emerge, AutoAnalysis will integrate their findings into the meta-analysis, providing cumulative evidence about when humans and AI perform better together and how human-AI performance varies across AI agents, tasks, and processes.

papers.title: SecPO: Principled Adversarial Training for Prompt Injection Security
papers.authors: Sizhe Chen, Yibo Peng, Jaewon Chang, Chawin Sitawarin et al.
papers.summary: Recognized as a top threat to AI agents, prompt injection allows instructions from untrusted data (email, documents, websites) to manipulate the agent's operation. The existing best-defended LLM, Meta-SecAlign, is trained with the DPO loss but still suffers from attack success rates (ASRs) approaching 100% under adaptive prompt injections. One reason is that DPO anchors the model around the undefended reference model, which is insecure. We show an idealized reference model—an injection-invariant, utility-preserving oracle—can nevertheless be approximated, as its output distribution in training is interestingly accessible. This new observation motivates a theoretically principled SecPO loss. Another Meta-SecAlign shortcoming is that it trains on weak simulated attacks. We implement an efficient adversarial training (AT) pipeline that synthesizes strong injected inputs (best@240), and train the model on them. Our AT reduces ASRs by 1.5-14.5× across three SoTA adaptive attacks, compared with Meta-SecAlign; the SecPO loss reduces them by a further 2.4-4.6× compared with using DPO loss. In agentic workflows, our SecPO + AT Qwen3.6-27B is much more secure than Meta-SecAlign: 8.8% vs. 78.8% AgentDojo ASR@800 under the AttackerMovesSecond attack. Moreover, our defended model shows no noticeable reduction in benign utility in nine benchmarks covering agentic tool calling, instruction following, science, and math. We release our //github.com/Sizhe-Chen/SecPOcode, //huggingface.co/datasets/Sizhe-Chen/Qwen3.6-27B-Instruct-SecPO-trainsettraining data (with optimized injections from AT), and //huggingface.co/Sizhe-Chen/Qwen3.6-27B-Instruct-SecPOmodel.

papers.title: Matching Workloads to Blackwell: Power-Resolved Benchmarking of NVIDIA B200 and B300 across HPC and AI Workloads
papers.authors: Mohsen Zand, Trung Dac Nguyen, H. Birali Runesha
papers.summary: We evaluate NVIDIA B200 and B300 (Blackwell Ultra) GPUs on two independent eight-GPU clusters, spanning computer-vision inference and training, LLM inference with Llama-3-8B and 70B llama3, and six production HPC codes. The B300 is not a uniform successor to the B200: it trails by up to 5.6× on convolutional inference, 8× on 3D vision transformer training, 24–27% on 70B LLM throughput, and 16× on double-precision Quantum ESPRESSO. We resolve the convolutional deficit using per-GPU board power rather than throughput alone: on the affected workloads the B300 draws only 36–53% of its 1100 W envelope, whereas on ViT-Large, which it wins, both parts saturate at 95–97% of TDP. Because our harness keeps inputs resident in device memory, a host-side data pipeline is excluded by construction, localizing the cause to per-kernel cost. Two B300 nodes of identical silicon differ by 2.1× in time-to-first-token solely from a development vLLM build. We give per-workload procurement guidance.

papers.title: Decentralized Dynamic Stable Matching
papers.authors: Jing Chen, Mengtong Gao, Zhenhe Zhang
papers.summary: We study decentralized computation of the player-optimal stable matching (POSM) with unannounced player arrivals and departures. Without a common clock, event information, or direct communication, players propose to arms and observe only their own accept/reject outcomes. Mismatch cost counts rounds when the realized matching differs from the current POSM. For known preferences, we give a deterministic polynomial-time self-calibrating protocol with cost O(t*+K² T), improving the previous bound O(T1-1/K( T)2/K). Here K is the number of arms, t* the last event time, and T the horizon. Players use only local time and proposal outcomes, knowing neither t* nor T. For any nondecreasing, polynomial-time-computable g(t)=Ω(t), the protocol achieves O(g(t*)+K²Ng(T)). Here g governs recovery time, while Ng(T) counts iterations of t t+g(t) below T, exposing a tradeoff between recovery time and asymptotic mismatch cost. Any randomized protocol with recovery scale g(t)1 and sublinear asymptotic mismatch cost has worst-case expected cost Ω(t*+Ng(T)). Thus, with g(t)=t, our protocol is optimal up to a K² factor among sublinear-cost protocols with O(t*) recovery time. For unknown preferences on both sides, each player and arm learns its preferences from its own observations after matching. We give a decentralized learning protocol with expected cost O(t*+K⁴Δmin⁻² T), where Δmin measures preference gaps. A complementary static-setting lower bound adapted from the literature shows that the dependence on T and Δmin is tight.

papers.title: How Much Can Tool Calls Reveal About You? Privacy Leakage from Tool-Call Traces
papers.authors: Donghang Duan, Qingyu Liu, Yifei Liu, Na Zou et al.
papers.summary: Large language model (LLM)-based agents interact with external tools through protocols such as the Model Context Protocol (MCP), producing tool-call traces that may expose behavioral signals about users. In this work, we systematically study the risk of user-profile inference from MCP tool-call traces, where observers infer user attributes from protocol-valid tool interactions without access to user conversations. We introduce PrivacyTrace, a benchmark containing 1,000 synthetic user profiles and 4,000 agent trajectories across four domains, generated with real MCP tools from 25 servers. Experiments with four mainstream LLM attackers show that tool-call traces enable a 26.25% attack success rate for profile inference, compared with 17.97% from prior-based guessing. Further analysis reveals that tool arguments and returned results provide the main trace-grounded evidence, while linking traces across sessions further amplifies profiling risk. These findings demonstrate that MCP tool-call traces can act as effective behavioral side channels for user profiling, motivating the development of privacy-aware mechanisms for agent-tool interactions. Code and data are available at https://github.com/AI45Lab/PrivacyTrace.

papers.title: No More Import Errors: Constrained Decoding for Guaranteed Valid Imports in LLM-Generated Tests
papers.authors: Konstantinos Kitsios, Matteo Biagiola, Guido Salvaneschi, Alberto Bacchelli
papers.summary: One of the most common failure reasons of LLM-based test generation pipelines is import errors. Grammar constrained decoding can modify the probabilities of the LLM's final layer during token generation to guarantee valid imports. However, we find that it can lead to degenerate solutions, i.e., repetitive valid imports (import streaks) that exhaust the token budget before a test is generated. We propose Constrained Beam Decoding with Lookup (CBDL), a novel method that guarantees import validity while addressing import streaks by avoiding premature commitment to tokens that lead to repetitive imports. Because it operates at the decoding stage, CBDL can be integrated into existing LLM-based test generation pipelines. We implement CBDL for Python and Java and evaluate it on two test generation tasks, showing that generated tests have 100% valid imports, outperforming both static (RAG and LIBRO) and dynamic (Agentic Repair) import-validity approaches that leave 45%, 10%, and 43% of import errors unresolved. CBDL converts on average 14% of initial import errors into functionally correct tests, increasing overall test correctness by 1-4 percentage points over unconstrained generation. Even when import validity does not directly lead to a correct test, it allows agentic repair pipelines to allocate the repair budget to remaining errors, increasing correct tests by 2-7 percentage points for Python and 1-6 for Java. Finally, we show that a hybrid pipeline, where a small local model equipped with CBDL generates imports while the frontier GPT-5.2 model generates the test body, outperforms generating both with GPT-5.2 alone by 1-3 percentage points. Overall, CBDL removes a major bottleneck in LLM-based test generation: by guaranteeing import validity with a small overhead (16-21 seconds per test), it improves test correctness and enables cost-effective hybrid generation.

papers.title: Self-Supervised Object-Centric Representation for Multi-Task Audio Analysis
papers.authors: Parthasaarathy Sudarsanam, Tuomas Virtanen
papers.summary: This paper studies the capability of an object-centric audio representation to support multiple downstream tasks within a unified framework. The object-centric model is trained in a self-supervised setup using slot attention by reconstructing Audio Spectrogram Transformer (AST) patch embeddings from a set of latent slots. It is trained on synthetic audio mixtures, which provides controlled multi-source audio scenes. These slot representations are evaluated for the classification, detection, and separation of sound events by training task specific output layers. On the classification task, the model achieves an F1-score of 0.8, comparable to clip-level AST embeddings which achieve 0.7. For sound event detection, it reaches a macro F1-score of 0.7, outperforming clip-level AST embeddings at 0.4 and matching AST patch embeddings at 0.7, which encode finer time-frequency information. In source separation, it achieves an SI-SDR improvement (SI-SDRi) of 18.4 dB. Furthermore, in a zero-shot source separation setting, the model achieves an SI-SDRi of 14.5 dB. These results demonstrate that slot-based representations capture transferable and compositional structure in audio scenes, enabling generalization across tasks and datasets.

papers.title: Stuck on Red? Understanding GitHub Actions Failing Streaks
papers.authors: Aref Talebzadeh Bardsiri, Tom Mens, Alexandre Decan, Thomas Degueule et al.
papers.summary: GitHub Actions is the de facto CI/CD service for GitHub repositories. Its workflows should not fail when they are not expected to, nor keep on failing too long. We empirically study failing streaks, i.e., uninterrupted series of failing runs of a workflow, in 30.9M+ runs of 154K+ workflows of 43K+ GitHub repositories over 238 days. We study how failing streaks begin and end, and what happens during them, based on the trigger and the commit of each run. We also classify all workflows by their purposes, such as building, testing or deploying, and we inspect the logs of a small sample of failing streaks. Failing runs mostly come in streaks: three quarters of them follow another failing run, and half of the workflows with at least three runs have at least one failing streak. Workflows serving multiple purposes have failing streaks more often, even at the same size. Most failing streaks end within hours, but the one in five that last more than a day account for the lion's share of the time that workflows spend failing. A third of the failing streaks start, and two in five end, without any change to the repository. In a sample of 100 failing streaks, those that end this way most often fail because of network issues or an external service. These findings suggest that maintainers should not assume that a failure comes from the last commit. GitHub and tool builders could flag failures that occur without any change to the repository, and alert the active maintainers when a workflow stays failing for more than a day.

papers.title: Layered Reproducibility for High-Performance Computing Applications: The Feel++ and Ktirio Urban Buildings Case Study
papers.authors: Javier Cladellas, Vincent Chabannes, Christophe Prud'Homme
papers.summary: The High-Performance Computing (HPC) community struggles with reproducibility due to complex software stacks, heterogeneous hardware, and expensive validation cycles. This contribution presents a layered reproducibility strategy in which Feel++ provides a traceable software supply chain and Ktirio Urban Buildings (KUB) builds on it to manage versioned urban-building data, executable simulations, and checksum-verifiable result artifacts. Feel++ treats continuous integration (CI) plans, CMake presets, packaging manifests, public software metadata, operations commands, containers, software bill of materials (SBOM)/provenance metadata, and Feel++ Benchmarking reports for Feel++ and KUB cases as repositoryowned artifacts. KUB applies this foundation to City Energy Model Database (CEMDB) datasets, manifests, Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable (FAIR) packaging, and verifiable outputs for computationally expensive simulations. The case study shifts reproducibility from late manual packaging to an artifact chain linking source commits, packages, containers, benchmark configurations, dataset versions, provenance records, and generated results.

papers.title: MFlowAudio: Efficient Text-to-Audio Synthesis via Mamba-based Stateful Flow Matching
papers.authors: Hao Dai, Panyu Chen, Jagmohan Chauhan
papers.summary: Recent advancements in audio generation have been largely driven by Transformer-based diffusion models. However, these models suffer from quadratic complexity of self-attention, severely bottlenecking the long-form audio synthesis. To overcome this limitation, we propose MFlowAudio, a novel latent audio generation framework that synergizes the continuous-time dynamics of Flow Matching with a custom-designed TCMamba backbone. TCMamba uses an innovative dual-scan mechanism: a TimeMamba module to capture long-range causal dependencies with linear complexity, and a ChannelMamba module to model cross-channel correlations such as harmonic structures. Exploiting this structural foundation, we formulate the Stateful Flow Matching (SFM) paradigm. This framework inherently enables chunk-wise training and streaming generation, maintaining an O(1) caching complexity without incurring extra computational overhead. To enable fine-grained controllable synthesis, we devise a novel guidance mechanism that neutralizes vector field collisions precipitated by on-the-fly semantic transitions of prompts. Comprehensive empirical evaluations confirm that MFlowAudio yields generative fidelity on par with state-of-the-art baselines while establishing significant computational efficiency, achieving above 14.5% acceleration in generation and facilitating perceptually seamless streaming synthesis with a constant latency of 1.8 seconds. Demo: https://huggingface.co/spaces/mflowaudio/MFlowAudio

papers.title: A Deterministic Commitment Rule over Unstructured DAGs for Optimistic Replication
papers.authors: João Paulo Bezerra, Petr Kuznetsov, Léo Olivier, Sara Tucci-Piergiovanni
papers.summary: In optimistic replication protocols, each replica uses the local state to execute requests from its clients in a wait-free manner, without synchronizing with other replicas. The outcomes may be revised later, making optimistic protocols only eventually consistent. To compensate for this consistency loss, an additional commitment mechanism can be employed: an underlying atomic broadcast protocol that allows replicas to periodically agree on the evolution of the object state. In this paper, we introduce a simple framework for optimistic replication based on a causality DAG: every replica represents the object state via a causally ordered set of client operations. The framework incorporates a deterministic commitment rule that incurs virtually zero message overhead beyond the basic dissemination of submitted operations.

papers.title: 6G-Enabled Cooperative Connected and Automated Mobility: Are We There Yet?
papers.authors: Mate Boban, Alessandro Bazzi, Claudia Campolo, Alexey Vinel et al.
papers.summary: Connected, cooperative, and automated mobility (CCAM) is a key enabler of future intelligent transportation systems, requiring seamless integration of communication, sensing, computing, and automation technologies. This paper surveys the state of the art in CCAM, focusing on key use cases and performance indicators, enabling technologies, system architectures, and standardization and regulatory developments relevant to large-scale deployment. Particular attention is given to cooperative perception, collective awareness, artificial intelligence and machine learning as fundamental building blocks of future CCAM ecosystems. The paper further identifies major research challenges related to scalability, interoperability, and real-time operation in highly dynamic mobile environments. Finally, it outlines future research directions toward achieving large-scale, safe, and resilient CCAM systems supported by next-generation communication networks.

papers.title: What Standard Evaluations Hide About Detectors of Hijacked LLM Agents: Rare Attacks, Unseen Tools and Benchmark Transfer
papers.authors: Mahmoud Abbasi, Juan M. Núñez V., Amin Shahraki
papers.summary: Detectors can flag hijacked large language model (LLM) agents from the traces of the tools they call. In the eleven evaluations we audited, attacks or anomalies make up 16% to 86% of the test samples, no evaluation varies that share, and six report no test on data from a second benchmark or source. We ask what such evaluations hide. On the AgentDrift and AgentDojo benchmarks we test trained detectors that read tool identities, behavior, call sequences, step embeddings or text, and a released LLM action monitor, AlignmentCheck, with thresholds fixed on training data or set by the monitor's released decision rule. First, at a 2% attack rate a detector with an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.879 reaches a precision of 0.076, and the mix of negatives alone moves that precision between 0.039 and 0.117. Second, as tool coverage, the share of test tool calls whose tool was seen in training, falls, detector rankings cross near 50% coverage and reverse below it, because unseen tools map to inputs that training never reached. Dropout on tool inputs largely removes the reversal. Third, no detector trained on AgentDrift ranks AgentDojo traces better than chance (AUROC 0.47 to 0.52), including one that reaches 0.996 within AgentDojo. The monitor, trained on neither, reaches 0.930, but with its open backbone its released decision rule would still mostly raise false alerts at a 2% attack rate (precision 0.096). We turn these findings into a checklist for evaluating trace detectors.

papers.title: Reparo: Synthesizing and Validating Access Control Policies
papers.authors: Ayesha Binte Mostofa, Gehao Zhang, Sam Stern, Juan Zhai et al.
papers.summary: Writing correct access control policies for software applications is difficult because it requires expertise in the authorization language and a thorough understanding of the application's authorization requirements. Existing synthesis and mining approaches assume explicit authorization inputs and a trusted reference policy. However, authorization logic is often distributed across code, comments, and documentation rather than captured in a single artifact, and developer-defined policies in real-world application repositories are often incomplete, outdated, or incorrect. We present Reparo, an LLM-aided pipeline for access control policy synthesis, repair, and validation. Reparo collects repository evidence for authorization intent and uses it to guide an LLM in generating an initial policy. It then uses official policy-language validation tools to identify and automatically repair errors. For semantic validation, a different LLM derives a behavioral oracle from the same repository evidence, consisting of concrete authorization requests with expected allow or deny decisions, which Reparo executes against the generated policy. We manually assess the oracle on a statistically sized sample of 390 test cases. We evaluate Reparo on 228 real-world GitHub repositories that use Cedar, OpenFGA, or Rego. In these repositories, 40.6-55.7% of the repository policies fail their language's validation tool, whereas Reparo produces 99.0-100% valid policies after repair. Agreement with the oracle is 98.2-99.6% for OpenFGA, 82.0-86.5% for Cedar, and 76.3-80.2% for Rego. Manual review confirms 91.5-96.9% of the sampled test cases as correct. Synthesizing and validating the policy for one repository takes about five minutes and costs 0.55-1.57. These results show that repository evidence can support both access policy synthesis and independent validation, even when no reliable reference policy exists.

papers.title: MERIDIAN: Memory-Encoded Rituals for Intimacy across Distance in an Interactive, Asynchronous Neighbourhood
papers.authors: Jingyi Chen, Yifan Yang
papers.summary: How can shared memories become playable structures for partners who live in different time zones? We present MERIDIAN, a pre-deployment design case of Yi Town, a bilingual browser game developed by one member of a long-distance couple as a gift for the other. Nine levels translate personally meaningful events, places and cultural references into tasks within a navigable pixel town. A birthday prologue and a fictional wedding frame the intended experience. Drawing on research through design, we reconstruct four design changes from 109 development commits, 28 changelog versions and three design specifications. These records support six situated design commitments, including memory-derived mechanics, staged access, local progress storage and bilingual coverage. The implementation combines a union-based progress model with manually exchanged, checksummed codes and time-zone-dependent scenery. An implementation audit reproduced 153 passing unit tests and examined all 1,024 canonical progress codes, while identifying limits involving resets, unversioned level registries and residual transcription errors. The application has no author-operated backend for progress, but external media services and browser speech recognition limit its privacy and offline guarantees. No recipient evaluation or relationship outcomes are reported. The contribution is an inspectable account of design decisions and their trade-offs, including the tension between authoring a personal gift and preserving the recipient's freedom to interpret, decline or reshape it. The game is playable at https://jingyifan.love and its source is public at https://github.com/rayford295/yi-town.

papers.title: From Training Exposure to Membership Evidence: A Controlled Study of OLMo 2
papers.authors: Ali Banaei, Muhammad Shahab Shahzad, Gerald Q. Maguire, Marco Chiesa et al.
papers.summary: Whether a language model was trained on a document matters for copyright, privacy, and benchmark contamination. Yet most membership-inference (MI) evaluations on language models collect members and non-members after the fact, so success may reflect distribution shift and failure is inconclusive. We re-ran OLMo 2 1B's official 50-billion-token mid-training stage, replacing selected training chunks with documents from 7,814 pairs matched on domain and difficulty. For each pair, a coin flip determined which document was inserted and which was held out. The run released by the Allen Institute for AI (AI2) from the same seed saw identical data everywhere else and serves as the counterfactual. One exposure raises a previously unseen document's likelihood on average but rarely identifies it. Using the counterfactual as reference, the reference ratio has an area under the ROC curve (AUC) of 0.767 but, with one threshold across domains, catches 3.8% of members at a 1% false-positive rate (FPR). In contrast, 13 matched pairs give a paired test 80% power at the 5% level to detect training on a collection, given same-domain non-members and a close reference. A reference trained with another seed recovers 92% of the counterfactual's AUC advantage over chance, whereas reference-free attacks stay within 0.07 of chance when pooled over domains. The full official post-training recipe, re-run on both models, leaves 89% of the average effect. Even with a closely matched reference, substantial document-level variability limits individual membership inference. We will release the checkpoints, per-token log-probabilities, and the evaluation documents; the code is available at https://github.com/ali-bana/OLMo-Twin.

papers.title: Simple Features Beat Most AI Control Monitors
papers.authors: Shubhrangshu Debsarkar, Valmik Nahata
papers.summary: AI control relies on monitors to catch a capable model that sabotages its work. These monitors are evaluated on their ability to differentiate honest from backdoored code. We show that on a standard evaluation dataset, simple features beat most monitors without ever running the code, outranking 20 of 24 open-weight models prompted as monitors. The dataset gives its labels away in two ways. People wrote the honest solutions and older language models the backdoors, so the style of the code reveals the class. Additionally, problems that LLMs can backdoor have different characteristics, so basic facts about the problem reveal it too. Swapping one class at a time for code by Claude Sonnet 5 shows that these features reward a contrast between authors, since human code against Sonnet 5's backdoors is easier to separate than the original pairs, 0.95 against 0.79. One in seven backdoors in the standard test set fails our validity checks, which distorts comparisons between attackers. A Sonnet 5 monitor appears to catch 77% of the older models' backdoors but 37% of Sonnet 5's, and 78% against 61% once both are verified. We do not show that published monitors rely on these shortcuts, but our findings suggest that a high score on such a dataset is not by itself evidence of sabotage detection. We release the rebuilt dataset and checks.

papers.title: A Failure Mode Taxonomy and Severity Model for Ethereum Smart Contracts
papers.authors: Fernando Richter Vidal, Naghmeh Ivaki, Nuno Laranjeiro
papers.summary: Smart contracts are a core component of blockchain systems, but their immutability makes failures in deployed code catastrophic and irreversible. Existing work classifies vulnerabilities, defects, and attacks, yet the observable failures of smart contracts, the deviations from intended behavior or the expected ledger state seen once a contract is deployed, have been largely disregarded. In this paper, we design and validate a failure mode taxonomy for Ethereum smart contracts, together with a severity model that ranks failures by their observable impact. Using a literature review as input, we follow the taxonomy development method of Nickerson et al. to derive the failure modes and their dimensions, and we subject the resulting taxonomy to a saturation exercise over a systematic literature review, the OpenSCV vulnerability catalog, and smart contract incidents reported after the search cutoff. Each failure mode is characterized along five dimensions, namely root cause, violated security property, impact (recorded as primary, secondary, and other), affected component, and nature, and is given a standardized name targeting the observable malfunction rather than the underlying vulnerability. From the taxonomy, we derive CIPER, a five-level severity model that groups failure modes by their observable impact. The saturation exercise produced no new failure modes or dimensions. The taxonomy offers a shared vocabulary for describing what smart contracts do wrong when they fail, and CIPER links that vocabulary to the severity of each observable outcome.

papers.title: Designing wearable haptic cueing for neurological gait rehabilitation: user requirements across residential care and community settings
papers.authors: Riasat Islam, Annemarie Zijlema, Theodoros Georgiou, Simon Holland et al.
papers.summary: Wearable haptic cueing offers rhythmic prompts for neurological gait rehabilitation while leaving hearing available for communication and environmental awareness. We investigated the user, design, and implementation requirements needed to make these systems usable in practice. We analysed six linked studies involving 17 people with neurological conditions affecting gait and three physiotherapists across formative sessions, residential care, and community self-management. Wearable devices served as technology probes. Observations, interviews, diaries, physiotherapist records, gait analysis, and activity logs informed thematic analysis and cross-study comparison. Seven recurring requirement areas concerned haptic perceptibility and placement, wearability and fastening, interaction burden, rhythm personalisation, real-world walking contexts, supported use, and perceived value beyond gait outcomes. Requirements interacted: perceptible cue locations could be difficult to access for fastening or control, while fixed rhythms did not always accommodate terrain, fatigue, interruptions, or changing pace. Carers and clinicians supported configuration, operation, safety, and interpretation. Participants described confidence, routine formation, and willingness to walk; these accounts were interpreted as perceived value rather than evidence of therapeutic efficacy. Low sensation, cognitive burden, and mobility limitations could make wearable cueing impractical. Future systems should offer adjustable haptic output, flexible placement, accessible fastening, simple controls, personalised rhythms, and robustness during everyday walking. Design should accommodate support from carers and clinicians and consider trade-offs between requirements. These findings inform wearable rehabilitation design rather than establish clinical efficacy.

papers.title: Look Over There! Dynamic Visual Guidance for AI-Narrated Slides
papers.authors: Jiongning Allen Lian, Yutong Alison Mei, Ho Ting Cheung, MK Michael Cheung et al.
papers.summary: Slides present information spatially, but narration unfolds linearly, leaving the viewer struggling to locate what the narration refers to. This split attention between audio and visual channels forces viewers to search the slide manually, imposing extraneous cognitive load and disrupting comprehension. The problem is especially acute on mobile devices, where dense layouts compressed onto small screens make visual search particularly effortful. In teacher-led settings, however, instructors naturally direct attention through pointing, pacing, and emphasis. Inspired by this, we present GuideSlide, a system that automatically generates Dynamic Visual Guidance for slide presentations, providing viewers with narration-synchronized visual cues that direct attention in real time. Given a PDF slide deck, GuideSlide automatically produces region-level zoom and time-aligned highlights without manual annotation. In a within-subjects study with 24 participants, GuideSlide substantially reduced perceived cognitive load and yielded higher immediate comprehension scores compared to static slides with identical narration. Participants strongly preferred the Dynamic Visual Guidance condition, reporting that it made narration easier to follow and reduced uncertainty about where to look. These findings suggest that narration-synchronized visual guidance is a valuable design strategy for slide-based presentations, with potential to extend to other instructional and presentation scenarios.

papers.title: What Carries Architectural Signal? A Code-to-Architecture Mapping Study
papers.authors: Rakhshanda Jabeen, Morgan Ericsson, Yuyao Duan, Anna Wingkvist
papers.summary: Code-to-architecture mapping assigns source files to modules of a reference architecture. Representations of implementation artifacts can capture code text, dependencies, and directory organization, but predictive gains alone do not establish the contribution of additional graph processing. Dependencies may already be encoded in these representations, while directories may closely match the reference decomposition. We investigate how artifact representations and graph context affect mapping on ten Java, C, and C++ systems with a limited labeling budget. We compare lexical, structural, and contextual file representations and assess each predictor with and without dependency neighbors. Using a Heterogeneous Graph Transformer (HGT), we compare file-level graphs extended with member nodes summarizing each file's program elements, folder nodes, or both, alongside a variant encoding folder paths directly in file representations. We compare folder-aware predictions with a directory rule using the same labeled files. Representations encoding dependency information outperform lexical representations on most systems. Additional neighbor aggregation can improve mapping, depending on the predictor and aggregation direction. Folder-aware variants yield the largest and most consistent gains across the evaluated HGT configurations. However, the directory rule achieves per-system median accuracy of 89-100%, and adding folder information does not consistently improve predictions for files the rule misclassifies. Member nodes provide no consistent improvement over file-level graphs. These findings support assessing what file representations and directory organization already provide before attributing improvements to graph neural networks.

papers.title: Self-Localization of Distributed Microphone Arrays Using One Source and Acoustic Reflections
papers.authors: Thomas Guffroy, Jean-Daniel Pascal Prieto, Cédric Foy, Antoine Deleforge
papers.summary: We present a method to estimate the relative position and orientation of two non-coplanar microphone arrays using a room impulse response (RIR) from a single source. The approach exploits early acoustic reflections, retrieved by each array in the form of a 3D image-source point cloud, using a recently-proposed image-source localization technique. The task is then reduced to aligning the two unlabeled point clouds, which is made difficult by their inherent symmetries and by spurious, missing and noisy estimates. To this aim we introduce ARCTIC, a point-cloud registration algorithm that performs a ranked search over congruent triangles anchored on the true source. Simulated and real experiments show that ARCTIC strongly outperforms two baselines, achieving mean angular and radial self-localization errors below 5 and 10 cm across 36 real RIRs measured in 6 different rooms.

papers.title: ARPEGE: Dataset and Methods to Estimate Acoustic and Geometric Parameters of Rooms from Sound
papers.authors: Jean-Daniel Pascal Prieto, Prerak Srivastava, Cédric Foy, Antoine Deleforge
papers.summary: Can one hear the walls of a room? To foster audio signal processing research around this question we release ARPEGE, a dataset containing hundreds of ambisonic spherical-array room impulse responses recorded in 6 empty rooms, annotated by the relative positions of sources, microphones and all acoustic reflectors. The dataset includes multiple room sizes, surface materials, orientations and distances, as well as recordings of human speakers and handclaps. Two state-of-the-art methods on image source localization and blind room parameter estimation are demonstrated on the data. Initial code for re-simulating the measured room impulse responses is provided, a longer term goal being to digitally twin the dataset.

papers.title: Scalable Audio-LLM System for Speech MOS Evaluation: A Diagnostic Case Study and Adaptation Roadmap
papers.authors: Dimitrios Kokkinis, Panagiotis Kakoulidis, Nikolaos Ellinas, Chrysovalanti Lymperi et al.
papers.summary: The continuous deployment of enterprise voice systems creates a critical operational bottleneck: evaluating the acoustic quality of synthetic speech across high-volume production updates. While human Mean Opinion Score (MOS) remains the quality gold standard, it introduces severe operational costs and turn-around delays that make continuous integration infeasible. In this work, we present a system design case study for a scalable, low-cost and offline evaluation pipeline capable of scoring large batches of synthetic speech at marginal cost. First, we use Qwen2-Audio-7B-Instruct in a zero-shot setting for granular MOS estimation, noticing perceptual blind spots and inherent biases. Then, we analyze SOMOS dataset and construct a diagnostic benchmark that operationalizes two prosodic dimensions associated with human naturalness ratings. Finally, we adapt Qwen2-Audio-7B-Instruct through a parameter-efficient finetuning (LoRA) on the task of MOS evaluation, observing improvements over base model and widely used neural baselines like UTMOS and establishing a practical blueprint for enterprise-grade speech quality assurance.

papers.title: Altered Visual Hand Feedback in Virtual Reality: An Exploratory Study in Essential Tremor
papers.authors: Alejandro Pascual-Valdunciel, Marcos Sacristán-Moraleda, Verónica Giménez de Béjar, Julián Benito-León et al.
papers.summary: Pathological tremor is the most prevalent movement disorder worldwide, characterized by involuntary muscular oscillations within a frequency of 3 to 12 Hz. Despite extensive research, the underlying mechanisms that generate and modulate tremor are not yet understood, and treatments are usually insufficient. While it is known that visual feedback is an important afferent pathway, little is known about the impact of altering the hand's visual representation on tremor expression. With the development of immersive technologies, VR poses an excellent tool to study how alterations to the representation of the hands affect tremor. In this work, we study this through two complementary experiments. In the first one, we show that a consumer-level hand-tracking system substantially attenuates tremor-band movements without preventing successful task completion. In the second one, with eight patients with essential tremor, we observe task-dependent differences in physical tremor between VR and the real world, with several patients exhibiting lower tremor-band activity in both hand kinematics and muscle oscillations, particularly during reaching tasks. Our findings represent an initial step toward validating the use of VR as an experimental tool for the research and treatment of pathological tremor, while highlighting strong user- and task-dependent effects.

papers.title: A prospective randomized study of patient-centered AI for clinical visit preparation
papers.authors: Xincheng Tan, Matthew Thompson, Xiang Ji, Angelica Willis et al.
papers.summary: Patients often arrive at brief, time-constrained clinical visits unsure of what to expect or ask, and millions of adults now turn to general-purpose AI chatbots to prepare beforehand. Yet whether conversational AI improves visit readiness remains unclear. We designed a large language model (LLM)-based visit preparation agent to guide patients before an appointment by gathering clinical context, setting visit expectations, providing relevant health information, building a prioritized list of questions for their clinician, and generating a summary. In a prospective consented randomized study in the Google Health app, 802 U.S. adults held 866 health-related conversations with the visit preparation agent (standard or concise variant) or a minimally prompted control chatbot built on the same LLM. The visit preparation agent significantly outperformed the control across blinded clinician evaluations and patient self-reports. In clinician reviews of completed sessions (n = 272), the agent achieved a 16.6% higher rate of comprehensive preparation (67.2% vs. 50.6%; P < 0.05) and an 8.5% higher rate of alignment with patients' health context (98.9% vs. 90.4%; P < 0.01), while maintaining high medical safety and appropriateness across all study arms. Patient post-surveys (n = 460) showed 16.8% higher visit preparedness (73.8% vs. 57.0%; P < 0.01), 14.3% higher confidence in knowing what to ask (81.4% vs. 67.1%; P < 0.01), and 12.0% higher overall satisfaction (74.0% vs. 62.0%; P < 0.05). Clinician and participant metrics were not significantly correlated, indicating that expert review and patient self-assessment capture complementary dimensions of patient-facing AI. These findings suggest that LLM chatbots can safely help patients prepare for clinical visits, with greater benefit when following a structured workflow, and motivate future studies on in-visit communication and clinical outcomes.

papers.title: Rome Wasn't Built in One Turn: Replay-Grounded Reward Signals for Long-Horizon Freeciv Agents
papers.authors: Yanchen Liu, Xinyu Che, Brihi Joshi, Renzo Fukuda et al.
papers.summary: Training language-model agents to play long-horizon strategy games is hard because deterministic feedback is sparse and often arrives only at the end of a game. In-game scores can offer dense signals, but they do not reliably predict future outcomes: in 8-68% of position pairs across eight strategy games, the higher-scoring position leads to the worse outcome. We term this phenomenon scoreboard traps. In Freeciv, an open-source turn-based empire-building game where several players manage units, cities, and diplomacy over hundreds of turns, we look into better reward signals for gameplay agents. To facilitate this, we build CivHarness, an open system that saves current game states, branches on different decisions, and replays the game to future turns to provide measurable long-horizon feedback from saved positions. We use CivHarness to train CivTelescope, an LLM Judge that predicts which one of two game positions will yield the better outcome. On scoreboard-trap pairs, CivTelescope is 1.3-2.0 times more accurate than off-the-shelf language models, and it generalizes to new game starts, later turns, and unseen rules. We then train a Freeciv gameplay agent with CivTelescope as a dense reward, and call this recipe CivMarshmallow. When used in the middle stage of the game where scoreboard traps are common, CivMarshmallow reaches an average training phase gain of 8.94 points, 77% more than the best baseline, the end-of-game reward. Over the full 120-turn game, CivMarshmallow uses a hybrid reward that starts from the scoreboard or the end-of-game reward and shifts to CivTelescope as the game advances; this hybrid reward scores highest among the rewards we compare.

papers.title: Payroll Fraud Detection in Synthetic HR/ERP Graphs: An Inductive Comparison of Rules, Path Features, and Graph Neural Networks
papers.authors: Xiaobo Chen, Genliang Zhu, Ziyuan Wang, Chu Wang
papers.summary: Payroll-fraud screening requires finding hidden employee–payee links while distinguishing suspicious relationships from legitimate ones. We formulate this problem as inductive link prediction and entity ranking on synthetic human-resources and enterprise resource planning (HR/ERP) graphs, with unseen organizations and a matched benign twin for every planted case. An original study on 24 held-out organizations and a prospectively frozen extension compare analyst rules, explicit path features and graph neural networks (GNNs). A tuned gradient-boosted model on chained-join features achieved the highest overall link average precision (AP; 0.823), above the GraIL-style GNN (0.663); its 4-hop AP was 0.646 versus 0.272. Thus, the observed multi-hop gain is not specific to GNNs. On a new synthetic cohort with 2.0% positive entities, chained-join boosting again led (AP 0.798); the relational entity GNN also exceeded record-aware rules (0.707 versus 0.504). At a 2% review budget, their precision was 0.695 versus 0.602. Under 40% failed identifier joins, the entity GNN ranked above chained-join boosting (AP 0.712 versus 0.683, descriptively). Structure-only auditing exposed a shortcut in the initial generator; matched twins reduced the audited twin-pool AUROC to 0.493–0.514. These results separate multi-hop candidate discovery, record-based discrimination and review prioritization within an explicit synthetic evaluation design. Code and data are available from the authors on request.

papers.title: Evaluating Structural and SAT Attack Resilience in Cryptographic Dynamic Logic Locking via Keystream Capping
papers.authors: Nahush Tambe, Naseeruddin Lodge, Vineet Chadalavada, Fareena Saqib
papers.summary: Untrusted third-party entities throughout the semiconductor supply chain expose proprietary hardware intellectual property to reverse engineering, piracy, and overproduction. While logic locking counters this threat by embedding key-dependent logic, conventional static key-gates remain vulnerable to both oracle-guided SAT attacks and structural removal attacks due to their time-invariant netlist signatures. Dynamic schemes such as STREAMLOCK mitigate oracle attacks by continuously masking signals with cryptographic keystream, achieving near 50% Hamming distance output corruption under incorrect keys with low hardware overhead. However, confining key-gates to primary outputs leaves internal combinational cones vulnerable to single-tap structural bypasses. This work extends dynamic logic locking by distributing key-gates within internal paths prioritized via fault-propagation analysis. The original and internally-hardened architectures are evaluated against structural removal attacks and a bounded, unrolling-based SAT-style attack across three ISCAS'85 benchmarks. Distributing masking internally raises the uninformed attacker's brute-force search space from 6 candidate node subsets to over 10⁴⁵ for the largest benchmark. Crucially, empirical analysis reveals that topological relocation alone does not prevent algebraic key extraction when wide circuits expose numerous keystream bits per clock cycle. To eliminate this leak, a keystream-bit reuse cap is introduced to restrict per-cycle exposure independent of circuit width. Under this constraint, SAT-solver tractability encounters an immediate computational cliff, transitioning sharply from rapid under-constrained solving to timeout thresholds without disclosing the secret key. Integrating fault-aware internal placement with keystream reuse capping delivers joint resilience against structural bypasses and bounded SAT attacks.

papers.title: Optimization Techniques for Solving the Minimum Red–Blue Separating Set Problem with an Application to Human–AI Text Separation
papers.authors: Marko Djukanović, Staša Vujičić Stanković, Žiga Zebec, Christian Blum
papers.summary: We study the so-called Minimum Red''Blue Separating Set Problem (MRBSSP) which arises from computational geometry. In particular, we propose a compact Set-Cover ILP formulation, safe preprocessing rules, a Greedy Randomized Adaptive Search Procedure (GRASP), and two exact approaches: one is based on Logic-Based Benders Decomposition (LBBD) approach, and the second represents a novel Branch-and-Benders-Cut (BBC) approach. These two exact approaches are compared to ILP–alongside GRASP and the Variable Neighborhood Search (VNS) from literature. Experiments on 250 random graphs with up to 500 vertices reveal complementary strengths: ILP yields the best feasible solutions, LBBD provides the strongest lower bounds and smallest mean optimality gap, and BBC certifies optimality most frequently. We further introduce an NLP application distinguishing human- and AI-generated texts through vocabulary-based graph features. On 42 instances, BBC achieves the smallest mean optimality gap, certifying 16 optima, while GRASP outperforms VNS. Structural analysis of optimal vocabulary separators identifies 113 mandatory and 151 replaceable features across 272 tests, highlighting substantial variability among optimal solutions. Overall, our results demonstrate the effectiveness of complementary optimization strategies and the interpretability of optimal vocabulary-based discrimination.

papers.title: Grounding Image Composition with Label-Conditioned Visual Evidence
papers.authors: Armin Dadras, Tingyu Lin, Robert Sablatnig, Franziska Proksa et al.
papers.summary: Image composition labels such as center, diagonal, or rule of thirds describe visual structure rather than object categories. KU-PCP provides image-level labels and class-specific geometric elements, but does not show which visible regions people associate with each of its nine classes. We introduce KU-PCP Elements (KU-PCPE), a label-conditioned region-evidence benchmark for photographic composition. Given an image and a label already judged applicable, the task is to segment the visible regions that explain why the label applies. KU-PCPE contains 4,093 single-annotator training masks and a 1,327-task expert test split with three masks per image-label task. The annotations also include exploratory segment-versus-line ratings that describe whether region or semantic-guideline evidence better explains the label. A held-out expert reaches .867 Dice against the other experts, while the strongest deployable model reaches .664, a proposal oracle .672, and the best vision-language model (VLM) proposal selector .395. KU-PCPE exposes the gap between recognizing a composition label and grounding the human-aligned visual evidence that makes it plausible in a particular image.

papers.title: EDU-Jev Training System-One Decision Models for Education
papers.authors: Jiazheng Li, Yulan He
papers.summary: Many automated decisions in education involve choosing from a fixed set of options: assigning a rubric score, checking whether an answer meets a marking criterion, or identifying the first wrong step in a solution.
